transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-11-29
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 42m
- Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luca (Optimize Eng); Marta (Cascade Head of ML), Ethan (Infra), Ravi (CTO)
- Recording: internal link (redwood-recording-..placeholder)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Redwood walked through Optimize recommendations, demoed Console prefetch configs and cost model sim. Customer asked about KV cache TTLs, session affinity, and how batching affects latency tail. Next steps agreed to run a perf job and exchange sample logs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jared: hey everyone, thanks for joining. um quick intros? we'll keep it focused on prefetch + sessionization because i saw your ticket saying high repeat prefixes in operator flows.
[00:12] Marta: yep that's right. our operators send very similar command prompts to the model, often the first 120 tokens are identical between sessions, then diverge. hoping to understand where caching helps.
[00:22] Priya: great, that's a classic prefix opportunity. we'll walk through the console prefs, the optimize cost sim, and then run a short back-of-envelope with your numbers. low-fidelity sim first, then priya will propose a benchmark.
[00:34] Ethan: one thing up front — we're leaning to hosted for speed but are worried about egress/data residency. also curious about dedicated if cost/latency looks better.
[00:44] Luca: totally — we'll cover routing and dedicated fallbacks. key concept: prefix/KV cache stores early key-values so you don't recompute the first N tokens per session. combined with prefetch (pipelines that fetch the KV for expected prefixes) you can avoid a lot of repeated work.
[00:58] Marta: when you say prefetch, you mean proactively loading a cached KV into the model server before the first token of a session arrives? i'm trying to picture the timing.
[01:07] Priya: yeah, essentially. imagine the operator clicks "start" and we already have the session id mapped to a cached prefix. the server fetches the KV into memory and warms the kv cache. then the very first generation call is just continuation, so latency for those initial tokens is much lower.
[01:22] Ravi: what's the hit-rate we need to see big wins? our prefixes vary a bit — there's templating with some variable fields.
[01:29] Priya: good Q. rough rule of thumb: >30% strong reuse gives sizable payback. if you can normalize templates (strip timestamps, IDs) you push hit rates way up. the cost model we use in the console shows savings curve under different hit rates — i'll share that.
[01:44] Ethan: what about TTLs and eviction — if we have 10k operators, how big does the cache get?
[01:51] Luca: cache sizing is workload dependent. we recommend LRU with a time-based TTL for session-like prefixes. also you can shard by customer or operator to isolate. in Dedicated pools you can reserve more memory for KV, which changes the economics.
[02:05] Jared: let's flip to the console demo — priya, can you share screen? (brief pause)
[02:20] Priya: ok sharing. this is a sample Optimize run for a customer with similar patterns. on the left i've loaded their session histogram — see lots of sessions under 6 utterances. that shapes batching strategy because small sessions make it hard to build big batches.
[02:40] Marta: yes, ours are short but frequent — operator issues come in waves.
[02:45] Priya: exact. so two levers: 1) prefetch/prefix cache to remove repeated first-token compute, and 2) micro-batching with concurrency shaping so you still get throughput without blowing p95 latency.
[02:58] Priya: here is the cost sim: baseline hosted with no cache, tokens-per-month X, cost Y. with a 45% prefix hit rate and prefetch enabled, we estimate ~48% token compute reduction and roughly 35% unit-cost saving after accounting for small prefetch overhead.
[03:18] Ethan: is that prefetch overhead network-bound? we have cross-region traffic concerns.
[03:24] Luca: the overhead is fetching the KV entry from the cache store — if your control plane is in the same region it's tiny. if cross-region you'll see higher latency and cost. that's one reason we suggest collocating cache storage or using Dedicated in region.
[03:36] Marta: can Redwood do on-prem/private cache? we have to keep some data inside our VPC.
[03:41] Jared: yes, Redwood Private supports a local KV cache (on-prem or VPC) and integrates KMS. for PCI or regulated data we typically recommend Private + VPC peering.
[03:50] Ravi: ok good. show us numbers on concurrency tradeoffs — we need p95 < 200ms for interactive operator flows.
[03:57] Priya: sure. here's a sim we ran: with prefetch+cache, single-request latency for cached sessions is median ~30ms faster because the model skip recompute for prefix. batching helps throughput but will increase p95 unless you cap wait windows. the console has a "latency budget" slider — set to 200ms and it will recommend batch size and max_wait_millis.
[04:19] Marta: can you explain max_wait_millis?
[04:22] Priya: it's how long the runtime will wait to form a batch before sending. lower = lower latency, but fewer token-level batching savings. the optimizer gives a suggested tradeoff curve; you pick the SLO and it outputs recommended settings + expected cost.
[04:33] Ethan: any rules for sessionization? our sessions sometimes have background telemetry plus operator note. do we treat telemetry as separate sessions?
[04:41] Luca: often you split machine telemetry into its own session and keep operator-initiated prompts as interactive sessions. that way the operator session benefits from prefix cache and you can cache the telemetry intents separately. Session affinity also affects KV reuse: sticky routing helps keep a session on the node with warmed KV.
[04:56] Ravi: sticky routing — does that block autoscaling? sounds risky.
[05:00] Priya: not necessarily. we use affinity that favors warm nodes but can fall back to other nodes if needed. autoscaler still works; it's just a soft preference. for Dedicated you can pin session shards to a subset of GPUs to maximize hit rate without impacting global autoscaling much.
[05:15] Marta: any practical examples of hit-rate impact?
[05:18] Priya: yes — sample: customer A with heavy prefix reuse saw 55% compute reduction; customer B with variable templates got 18% until they normalized templates and hit 40%. so prep work (normalization) can be big.
[05:32] Ethan: are there scenarios where prefetch makes things worse?
[05:36] Luca: if your prefetch rate is high but hit rate low, you pay overhead for fetching KVs that are never used. that's why we simulate using your session histogram — to set sensible TTLs and prefetch thresholds. also warm-up traffic patterns (bursts) can temporarily overrun memory if TTLs are too long.
[05:55] Marta: can we run a sample sim on our real logs? we'll scrub them but want realistic numbers.
[05:59] Jared: absolutely — that's the benchmark step. share a 1 week sample of session IDs and normalized prompts, and Priya will plug into Optimize.
[06:07] Marta: noted, we'll redact PII and send.
[06:09] (short pause, background noise)
[06:15] Priya: quick demo of console UI: here is the "prefetch policy" panel — fields: prefix_identifier (regex), min_hit_rate to enable prefetch, ttl_seconds, max_prefetch_concurrency. you can also choose "sessionize_by_cookie" or custom session key.
[06:34] Ethan: regex? so we'd need to set rules for templated prefixes. does Redwood help with that?
[06:38] Priya: yes, our DevRel/solutions folks can advise on normalization rules; often a few regexes catch 70-80% of templates. we'll include suggested regex patterns in the follow-up.
[06:50] Marta: on the cost-model, how do you account for quantization or smaller model fallback? we sometimes fall back to a tiny assistant for certain queries.
[06:59] Luca: the cost sim has model variants as inputs — you can model routing to smaller quantized variants on non-critical requests. it computes blended cost and expected quality delta. good place to put a tiny fallback for low-risk prompts.
[07:12] Ravi: what about consistency and hallucination risk when you use small fallback?
[07:16] Priya: that's an evaluation question — Optimize ties into your eval suites so you can run prompt sets and monitor quality regressions. if the fallback swings quality too much, the sim will show it.
[07:25] Marta: i'm also worried about concurrency limits from our side — do you throttle?
[07:28] Jared: Redwood exposes per-route quotas and per-key concurrency caps, plus token rate limits. part of the pilot we'll size those.
[07:36] (crosstalk)
[07:42] Ethan: one more infra Q — if we enable prefetch in hosted, where does the KV live?
[07:47] Luca: in hosted it's in regionally replicated cache managed by Redwood. you can opt for VPC-only KV in Private. for regulated data you should choose Private.
[07:58] Marta: good — our legal will ask.
[08:01] Priya: ok i'm going to walk through a short playback of the cost sheet using your estimated 1M tokens/month: baseline cost, then three scenarios (no cache, cache local + prefetch, dedicated with larger KV). see the blended per-token change.
[08:17] Priya: scenario 1: no cache — $X per month. scenario 2: prefetch + 40% hit rate — -37% compute cost, small prefetch IO cost, net -30% total. scenario 3: dedicated with 64GB KV memory reserved + prefetch at 60% hit — net -55% total unit cost but with committed capacity.
[08:39] Marta: commitment is ok if the numbers are clear. do you have a sample TCO calc?
[08:44] Jared: yes i'll include a TCO that spreads reserved vs on-demand cost over 12 months, includes egress and support.
[08:50] Ethan: what about tail-latency when cache cold-starts — any safety nets?
[08:54] Priya: we have fallback policies: synchronous cold compute (slower) or fast fallback to a smaller model; and we provide circuit-breaker metrics so you can alert if cold-start rate spikes.
[09:06] Marta: let's discuss benchmarks. what data do you need?
[09:09] Priya: 1) 1-week sample of sessions with normalized prompt text and session ids, 2) target SLOs (p50/p95/p99), 3) expected monthly token volume. with that we'll run a 1-hour synthetic workload that replays your trace across model variants and settings.
[09:25] Marta: ok we'll prepare and share via secure upload.
[09:28] Ravi: final — any security docs we can review? SOC2, KMS, data retention?
[09:33] Jared: yes i'll attach our SOC2 summary, KMS integration guide, and the Private deployment security checklist in the follow-up.
[09:40] (brief recap)
[09:45] Jared: quick recap: Priya will run bench and share console sim, Jared will send cost model + security docs, Marta will share sample logs. next call after bench to review results.
[09:57] Marta: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:00] (call closes)
